source_document.body:
For most manufacturers , the honest answer is no. A survey published in August 2026 found that 53% of manufacturing CEOs say their business could not keep running for three weeks during a major supply chain shock, and 80% believe up to a fifth of revenue would be at risk if their top three suppliers were disrupted for just two weeks. Closing that gap in 2027 does not start with buying more stock. It starts with better supplier management in direct materials procurement : data people can trust, visibility beyond the first tier and responses agreed before trouble arrives.
Why is supplier risk hiding beyond tier one?
What’s Related
Most manufacturers know their direct suppliers well; far fewer know who supplies those same suppliers. McKinsey’s latest supply chain risk survey found that 95% of companies can see risks at tier one, but only 42% can see into tier two or beyond. Unfortunately, that unmonitored area is also where the next disruption is most likely to start.
The practical first step for savvy procurement leaders to risk-proof the organization is not to take on the whole ecosystem, but to focus on the components and parts whose absence would actually stop the line. For each, they should build a short profile: approved suppliers and the sites they ship from, lead times, stock cover, qualified alternatives and a named owner. Then they should ask critical suppliers to disclose their own key sources.
RELATED STORIES: Five Things to Consider Before Deploying AI Agents in Procurement | AI Is Reshaping Procurement Jobs, But Few Leaders Have Redesigned Them
Can AI-powered procurement software close the gap in 2027?
It can, but only on solid foundations. Supplier and part data need a single owner and common identifiers across every plant and ERP system. Then AI -enabled procurement software earns its keep: reconciling duplicate records, mapping sub-tier suppliers, revealing where several critical parts converge on one source or port , and watching for financial distress, sanctions or logistics delays. People remain responsible for acting on what it finds, so it is important to set clear rules on what AI may recommend, what it may execute and who approves.
Michael Roesch
How will regulation reshape supplier collaboration next year?
Traceability is increasingly becoming a cost line. Since April 2026, US Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper apply to the full value of affected imports , and in August the UFLPA Entity List grew by 43 companies, including aluminum and copper producers. For businesses trading with Europe, the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) calls for traceability down to the individual plot of land for large and medium-sized operators, the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) has applied since 12 August 2026 and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) ill still require the largest companies to carry out supply chain due diligence from 2029. Building origin data into supplier onboarding and part records now is far cheaper than retrofitting it when a customer or customs officer asks.
What should manufacturers agree before the warning lights flash?
Most manufacturers monitor supplier risk; fewer have decided what happens when an alert fires. For each trigger, whether a quality failure, a sanctions listing, a cyber incident or a port delay, it is important to agree who responds, what action follows and which alternatives are already qualified.
Cost, risk, resilience and compliance will still define supply chain performance in 2027. What will separate manufacturers is how early they spot trouble and how quickly they act. The route isn’t exciting new kit: tidy the data, map the supply base, connect planning to sourcing and agree the rules for people and machines alike. Those who start now will be best placed when the next shock arrives.
Michael Roesch is General Manager, Manufacturing at JAGGAER
